title: Bella Vista Bistro: fraud risk assessment, internal control weaknesses and an ethical response
participant_role: Outside accountant at a small CPA firm reviewing a restaurant client's cash and vendor records
judge_role: Owner of Bella Vista Bistro, who trusts a long-time office manager and is shocked by the accountant's findings

difficulty.rationale: Fraud triangle, control weaknesses and loss estimate; mostly reasoning.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of an outside accountant at a small CPA firm. The owner (judge) of BELLA VISTA BISTRO, a family restaurant and long-time client, has asked you to explain some unusual results you found while preparing the third quarter financial statements.

Dana, the office manager, has worked at the restaurant for eight years and is completely trusted by the owner (judge). Dana has never taken a vacation and recently bought a new car. Dana opens the mail, prepares the bank deposits, posts all transactions to the books, adds new vendors to the accounting system, prepares checks and stamps them with the owner's (judge's) signature stamp, and reconciles the bank account each month. The owner (judge) focuses on the kitchen and the dining room and rarely looks at the books.

While preparing the quarterly statements, you compared the point of sale (POS) reports to the bank deposits, reviewed voided sales and looked at the vendor payment history. Your findings are shown below.

[Exhibit A: Q3 cash sales vs cash deposited; Exhibit B: voided cash sales in Q3; Exhibit C: new vendor DK Supply: see exhibits]

The owner (judge) is upset and wants your honest assessment and advice on what to do next.

You must:
- Assess the fraud risk using the fraud triangle
- Quantify the possible loss
- Identify the internal control weaknesses
- Recommend internal control procedures for the restaurant
- Explain how the owner should respond appropriately

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the restaurant's back office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Assess the fraud risk using the fraud triangle
Recommend internal control procedures for the restaurant
Explain how the owner should respond appropriately

exhibits.title: Exhibit A: Q3 POS cash sales vs cash deposited
Exhibit B: Voided cash sales in Q3
Exhibit C: New vendor DK Supply

judge_questions: Dana has been with me for 8 years. Shouldn't I just talk to her?
I'm a small restaurant. I can't afford to hire more office staff. What controls can I realistically use?

solution.overview: A strong answer uses the fraud triangle to show that all three conditions are present, adds up a possible loss of up to $11,400 (still to be confirmed) and explains that one person controls custody, recording and reconciliation. The presenter recommends practical controls organized around the five components of internal control and advises the owner to respond carefully: preserve records, restrict access and bring in a forensic accountant instead of confronting Dana alone.

answer: Pressure: a new car and possible personal money problems
Opportunity: Dana handles cash, records and reconciliation with no review, and uses the signature stamp
Rationalization: long tenure may lead to thinking "I'm underpaid" or "I'll pay it back"
Red flags: never takes a vacation, lifestyle change, unusual voids, a vendor with a P.O. box and no purchase orders
All three sides are present, so fraud risk is high
Deposits short $900 each month x 3 = $2,700
Excess voided cash sales by Dana = $3,150
DK Supply payments 3 x $1,850 = $5,550
Potential exposure up to $11,400, to be confirmed by investigation (voids and short deposits may overlap)
No segregation of duties: one person has custody of cash, records transactions and reconciles the bank
No mandatory vacation, so nobody else ever sees Dana's work
Dana can add vendors with no approval or verification
Signature stamp lets checks go out without the owner seeing them
Voids need no manager approval, and the owner does not review the books
Control environment: owner sets the tone by reviewing reports and signing checks personally (or dual approval)
Risk assessment: identify cash, voids and vendor payments as high-risk areas

Control activities: separate duties (owner opens the bank statement, someone else reconciles), manager approval for voids, owner approves new vendors with a W-9 and address check, daily deposit matched to the POS Z-report
Information and communication: POS void and discount reports sent to the owner each week
Monitoring: mandatory vacation and job rotation, periodic outside review, fidelity bond or crime insurance
Treat this as an allegation until proven; do not accuse or confront Dana alone
Preserve records (POS data, bank statements, vendor files) before anything is changed
Quietly restrict Dana's system access and take back the signature stamp
Engage a forensic accountant and an attorney, and notify the insurer
Ethical dilemma: loyalty to a trusted employee vs the duty to protect the business and report facts honestly

calculations.label: Voids comparison
steps: Other staff: about 3 voids and about $120 each person
Dana voids about 14 times as often as a typical employee (42 / 3)

judge_question_answers.question: Dana has been with me for 8 years. Shouldn't I just talk to her?
answer: Not yet: a conversation could lead to records being changed or destroyed
Secure the evidence and restrict access first, then let a forensic accountant or attorney plan any interview
The findings are red flags, not proof; there may be an explanation, so be fair and factual
Handling it properly protects both the business and Dana

judge_question_answers.question: I'm a small restaurant. I can't afford to hire more office staff. What controls can I realistically use?
answer: Owner oversight costs little: open the bank statement yourself, sign checks personally and approve new vendors
Use technology: POS alerts for voids, a bank app to view deposits daily, positive pay for checks
Require manager approval for voids and match each day's deposit to the POS Z-report
Require vacations, and have the CPA firm do the bank reconciliation or a monthly review

key_concepts.definition: The three conditions usually present when fraud occurs: pressure (a need or motive), opportunity (weak controls) and rationalization (a way to justify it).
The policies and procedures a business uses to protect assets, keep accounting records accurate, promote efficiency and follow laws and management's rules.
Splitting custody of assets, recording of transactions and authorization or reconciliation among different people so one person cannot commit and hide an error or theft.
Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring (the COSO framework).
Stealing cash before or after it is recorded, often hidden by voiding sales or depositing less than the POS shows.
A fake vendor is added to the system so the company pays invoices for goods or services never received. Red flags include P.O. box addresses and no purchase orders.
Warning signs of possible fraud, such as an employee who never takes vacation, a sudden lifestyle change, unusual voids or unexplained vendors.
Requiring employees to take time off and letting others perform their duties so hidden schemes are likely to surface.
Insurance that reimburses the business for losses caused by employee theft or dishonesty.
An accountant trained to investigate suspected fraud, gather evidence properly and measure losses for legal or insurance purposes.
A situation where two values conflict, such as loyalty to a trusted employee and the duty to protect the business and act on the facts.

notes: State level because there are no journal entries to hide behind: students must connect the numbers to the fraud triangle, the five components of internal control and a professional, ethical response. Common mistakes are telling the owner to fire or confront Dana immediately, calling it proven theft, and recommending hiring more staff instead of low-cost owner oversight and technology.

criteria.exceeds: Walks through all three sides of the fraud triangle (pressure: the new car; opportunity: Dana controls cash, records, reconciliation and the signature stamp; rationalization: long tenure), names the red flags, and totals a possible loss of up to $11,400 ($2,700 short deposits + $3,150 voids + $5,550 DK Supply) while noting the voids and short deposits may overlap and must be confirmed.
criteria.meets: Uses the fraud triangle to conclude that fraud risk is high and adds up a possible loss of $11,400 from the three exhibits.
criteria.below: Names only one or two sides of the fraud triangle, or misses part of the loss (for example leaves out the $5,550 paid to DK Supply) or calls the $11,400 proven theft.
criteria.little: Does not assess fraud risk or quantify any loss, or says there is nothing unusual in the exhibits.

items.label: Explain the purpose of internal accounting controls

criteria.exceeds: Explains that controls protect assets and keep records accurate, then shows how the missing controls (no segregation of duties, no mandatory vacation, Dana adding vendors, the signature stamp, voids with no approval, no owner review) let one person both take cash and hide it.
criteria.meets: States that internal controls protect assets and keep records accurate, and identifies the lack of segregation of duties and the other main weaknesses at Bella Vista.
criteria.below: Gives a general definition of internal control but identifies only one or two weaknesses, or does not link them to the problems in the exhibits.
criteria.little: Cannot explain why controls matter, or identifies no control weaknesses.

items.label: Determine the components of internal accounting control procedures for a business

criteria.exceeds: Organizes recommendations around the five components (control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, monitoring) with specific restaurant procedures such as manager approval for voids, owner approval of new vendors with a W-9 and address check, and daily deposits matched to the POS Z-report.
criteria.meets: Recommends practical control activities for cash, voids and vendor payments, such as separating duties, approving voids and new vendors, and having the owner sign checks or review the bank statement.
criteria.below: Recommends only one or two controls, or gives general advice ("watch the books more") without specific procedures.
criteria.little: Recommends no controls, or suggests something that does not address the weaknesses found.

criteria.exceeds: Explains how controls stay effective over time: weekly POS void and discount reports to the owner, mandatory vacation and job rotation, a monthly review or bank reconciliation by the CPA firm, and a fidelity bond or crime insurance, all at low cost for a small restaurant.
criteria.meets: Recommends ongoing monitoring such as mandatory vacations, the owner reviewing reports and bank statements regularly, and a periodic outside review.
criteria.below: Sets up controls once but gives no plan for reviewing or monitoring them, or relies on hiring more staff.
criteria.little: Does not address how controls will be maintained.

items.label: Recognize and respond to ethical dilemmas

criteria.exceeds: Names the dilemma (loyalty to a trusted employee versus the duty to protect the business and report facts honestly) and lays out a fair response: treat it as an allegation, preserve records, quietly restrict Dana's access and take back the signature stamp, then bring in a forensic accountant, an attorney and the insurer.
criteria.meets: Advises the owner not to confront Dana alone, to preserve records and restrict access, and to involve a forensic accountant.
criteria.below: Gives a partly appropriate response, for example suggests firing Dana right away or treats the red flags as proof of theft.
criteria.little: Does not recognize the ethical issue, or advises ignoring the findings or confronting Dana immediately.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects each exhibit to a scheme and a weakness: $900 short every month and 42 voids (about 14 times a typical employee) point to skimming, and DK Supply with a P.O. box and no purchase orders points to a fake vendor.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the three exhibits to a high fraud risk and a possible loss of $11,400.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how the weaknesses allowed the losses.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the owner a clear, ordered plan (secure evidence, restrict access, call a forensic accountant, then add low-cost controls) that fits a small restaurant that cannot hire more office staff.
criteria.meets: Makes clear recommendations for both the investigation and the new controls.
criteria.below: Recommendations are vague, out of order, or rely on hiring more staff.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or tells the owner to do nothing.

criteria.exceeds: Delivers upsetting findings to the owner calmly, factually and respectfully, in plain language, with a logical order from risk to loss to controls to next steps.
criteria.meets: Presents the fraud triangle, loss estimate, weaknesses and recommendations clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or sounds accusatory toward Dana.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a clear visual such as a fraud triangle drawing or a table matching each duty to a different person, and suggests low-cost technology ideas like POS void alerts, a bank app for daily deposits and positive pay.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the risks and controls easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or practical.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: not to talk to Dana yet because records could be changed, secure evidence first and let a forensic accountant or attorney plan any interview since the findings are red flags, not proof; and suggests low-cost controls such as opening the bank statement, signing checks, approving vendors, POS void alerts, positive pay, matching deposits to the Z-report, required vacations and a CPA monthly review.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including waiting to talk to Dana until evidence is secured and naming several low-cost owner oversight controls.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers such as "hire someone" or "just ask her."
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or advises confronting Dana alone right away.

key_points: All three sides of the fraud triangle are present (pressure, opportunity, rationalization), so fraud risk is high
Short deposits: $900 a month x 3 = $2,700; Dana's voids: 42 totaling $3,150; DK Supply: 3 x $1,850 = $5,550
Possible loss of up to $11,400, to be confirmed by investigation (voids and short deposits may overlap)
Core weakness: no segregation of duties, since Dana has custody of cash, records transactions and reconciles the bank
Controls organized by the five components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, monitoring
Low-cost controls: owner opens the bank statement and signs checks, manager approves voids, owner approves new vendors, daily deposit matched to the POS Z-report, mandatory vacation
Do not confront Dana alone: preserve records, restrict access, take back the signature stamp, and engage a forensic accountant, an attorney and the insurer
